message.abstract: <jats:p>Homeostatic reinforcement learning provides a framework for understanding adaptive feeding through the regulation of internal physiological states, yet the computational origins of dysregulated feeding remain poorly understood. Here, we develop a reinforcement-learning framework in which an agent learns adaptive feeding from physiological consequences in a partially observable environment with delayed and overlapping dynamics. During learning, a low-dimensional physiological representation emerges within the network that contains information related to hunger and fullness despite receiving no direct supervision for either signal, providing an interoception-like internal state for feeding control. We then identify two distinct levels at which this learned regulation can be disrupted. At the representation level, perturbing the learned interoceptive state creates a faulty state, causing the agent to act on systematically distorted physiological information and resulting in under- or over-eating. At the learning level, selectively attenuating positive or negative temporal-difference errors during retraining creates faulty learning, producing distinct dysregulated feeding phenotypes while leaving the physiological representation otherwise intact. Thus, similar behavioral phenotypes can arise from distinct computational failures: how physiological state is represented and how the consequences of actions are learned. This framework provides a computational basis for distinguishing representation-level and learning-level mechanisms underlying dysregulated feeding.</jats:p>
title: Faulty States, Faulty Learning: Distinct Routes to Dysregulated Feeding in Homeostatic Reinforcement Learning
